name: The Legal Ground
title: The Legal Ground
answer: The legal ground for English learners is the body of federal statutes and court decisions that require schools to help students overcome language barriers and give them meaningful access to grade level content. In August 2025 the Department of Education rescinded a 2015 guidance letter on those duties, but the rescission changed the guidance and not the law. Schools still owe these students the same obligations, and leaders should check current state guidance before relying on any federal resource.

sections.body: Schools have carried legal duties toward English learners for decades, and those duties come from Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, the Supreme Court's decision in Lau v. Nichols, and the Castañeda v. Pickard standard. A 2015 letter from the Departments of Education and Justice explained in detail how schools could meet those duties, which gave leaders a practical picture of what compliance looked like. In August 2025 the Department of Education withdrew that letter, saying it did not align with the administration's priorities. The problem this idea addresses is the confusion that follows, because a withdrawn guidance document can easily be mistaken for a withdrawn obligation. The idea is that the underlying law did not move when the guidance did, so schools must keep serving English learners while watching for further changes.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not divide this work by grade band, so the same duties apply across a school. Districts should watch their state education agency for guidance and check the status of federal changes before relying on any federal resource. Every Student Succeeds Act requirements for English learners still apply, and many states have their own laws on English learner education. Whatever the grade level, schools still owe English learners meaningful access to grade level content. Leaders should keep that obligation at the center of planning while the federal picture shifts.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text presents no research evidence for this idea. It rests instead on legal and policy sources: Education Week in 2025 for the rescission and for the point that the letter was not legally binding and the statutes and court decisions it described remain in place, Colorín Colorado in 2025 for the continuing Every Student Succeeds Act requirements and state laws, and Education Week in 2026 for the Department of Education's April 2026 notification to Congress that it planned to dissolve its Office of English Language Acquisition. No study or figure is given. Treat this as a description of the legal and policy landscape rather than a body of research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here concern what a school can and cannot lean on. The 2015 letter was not legally binding, so its withdrawal does not by itself change what schools must do, and the text warns against relying on any federal resource without checking its current status. The federal office that oversees English learner programs is in flux, and the Department of Education notified Congress in April 2026 that it planned to dissolve the Office of English Language Acquisition, though advocates note that schools' federal duties remain with or without that office. Districts should look to their state education agency for guidance. Decisions about how to serve English learners stay with schools and their leaders, who must still provide meaningful access to grade level content.
